faq.a: Killing parasites releases merozoite antigens and free hemoglobin, triggering immune‑mediated destruction.
faq.q: Why does hemolysis worsen after starting antimalarials?

faq.a: No; parasites may be sequestered. Treat based on clinical picture and recent positive test.
faq.q: Can a negative malaria smear rule out malaria‑associated hemolysis?

faq.a: Only in fulminant hemoglobinuric renal failure unresponsive to standard transfusion and hydration.

exam: A patient with falciparum malaria develops sudden jaundice and Hb 6 g/dL – what is your next step? — Check smear, start IV artesunate, arrange urgent transfusion.
How does G6PD deficiency alter malaria treatment? — Avoid oxidative drugs (primaquine, quinine); use artesunate and monitor hemolysis.
Differentiate malaria‑induced hemolysis from sickle‑cell crisis on smear and history. — Presence of parasites, reticulocytosis, and lack of painful crises point to malaria.
Why is LDH more reliable than bilirubin in early hemolysis? — LDH rises immediately with cell lysis, bilirubin lags behind.
What are the WHO criteria that classify severe malaria with hemolysis? — Hb < 7 g/dL, bilirubin > 3 mg/dL, renal impairment, or high parasite load.
Explain why you would give a blood transfusion before completing a full malaria work‑up. — Life‑threatening anemia must be corrected urgently; antimalarial therapy can start empirically.
What complications can arise from untreated malaria‑associated hemolysis? — Acute kidney injury, severe anemia, cardiovascular collapse.
How would you manage hemolysis if laboratory LDH is unavailable? — Use clinical signs (jaundice, dark urine), monitor hemoglobin trend, and treat aggressively.
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Severe malaria can cause intravascular hemolysis leading to anemia, jaundice and renal injury. Recognise the pattern, use limited investigations, and start prompt antimalarial and supportive care.

b: Acute drop in hemoglobin >2 g/dL within 24 h
Elevated lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) and indirect bilirubin
Reduced haptoglobin
sections.p: Plasmodium falciparum and, less often, P. vivax invade red cells, triggering immune‑mediated and direct parasite destruction. Hemolysis peaks 48‑72 h after treatment but may start before therapy.

b: Distinguish hemolysis from bone‑marrow suppression (reticulocytosis present)
Assess severity: Hb < 7 g/dL, bilirubin > 3 mg/dL, or rising creatinine
Identify precipitating factors: G6PD deficiency, quinine‑induced oxidative stress, herbal remedies
sections.p: Hemolysis is part of severe malaria (WHO criteria) and can coexist with other complications such as cerebral malaria or acute kidney injury.

b: History of recent malaria exposure or treatment
Examination: scleral icterus, splenomegaly, tachycardia
Watch for signs of shock: hypotension, altered mental status
sections.p: Patients present with pallor, dark urine, jaundice and sometimes abdominal pain. Rapid recognition prevents fatal anemia and renal failure.

t.b: Confirms malaria species and parasite density; also shows schistocytes if mechanical hemolysis
Shows falling hemoglobin, reticulocytosis; if unavailable, use clinical anemia assessment
Quantifies hemolysis; if labs missing, rely on jaundice and dark urine
Detects hemoglobinuric acute kidney injury; if no lab, monitor urine colour and volume
Identifies risk for drug‑induced oxidative hemolysis; if unavailable, avoid primaquine/quinine in high‑risk groups

b: IV artesunate (WHO first‑line) – kills parasites rapidly
Avoid quinine in known G6PD deficiency or severe oxidative stress
Transfuse packed RBCs if Hb < 7 g/dL or symptomatic
Hydration and diuretics to prevent pigment nephropathy
Monitor electrolytes, renal function, and repeat smear after 24 h
sections.p: Treat the malaria first, then support the hemolysis.

Severe bacterial sepsis with DIC – consumptive coagulopathy, low platelets
Drug‑induced hemolysis from antimalarials (e.g., primaquine) – occurs after exposure
sections.p: Other causes of acute anemia in the tropics.
